tool_summary: Transfers data to/from servers over HTTP(S) and other protocols. The classic curl-pipe-to-shell pattern (curl ... | sh) is one of the most common install-script vectors on the internet; -o can write fetched content anywhere the invoking user can write.
platform_notes: curl behavior and flags are consistent across Linux and macOS.

rules.description: Piping curl's output directly into a shell (curl ... | sh, curl ... | bash, or via `sh -c "$(curl ...)"`) executes fetched remote content immediately, with no opportunity to review it first. This is one of the most common supply-chain and drive-by-install patterns on the internet, legitimate and malicious alike.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends entirely on what the fetched script does, which commandant does not inspect. Treated as the worst case since the content is never reviewed before executing.
rules.notes: This rule's raw_pattern matches the direct pipe form (curl ... | sh) only. The command-substitution variant (sh -c "$(curl ...)") is not matched by this pattern; it would need to be caught by sh.json's -c destructive-payload rule inspecting the substituted content, which itself only sniffs for a small set of known-dangerous string patterns rather than recognizing curl-fetch-and-execute as its own category. This is a real coverage gap, not an oversight in wording.

rules.description: The -k/--insecure flag disables TLS certificate verification, removing protection against man-in-the-middle interception or spoofed servers for this request.
The -o/-O/--output flags write the fetched response body to a local file, which can overwrite an existing file without confirmation depending on the destination.
rules.reversible_note: If the destination file already existed, its prior contents are overwritten and not recoverable by curl itself.

rules.description: Transfers data to or from a server. A bare request without output redirection or piping to a shell is low risk.
